title: Chinese regulators tell Tesla to fix nearly 3 million cars
gist: Chinese regulators are forcing Tesla to recall 2.98 million Model 3/Y vehicles over electronic door-handle safety after fatal crashes, plus a separate 2.74 million-car recall to upgrade driver-monitoring from a steering-wheel torque sensor to camera-based gaze tracking -- with reports that the current system can already be fooled by a doll's head.

themes.theme: China cracks down on electronic door handle safety

insights.claim: Chinese regulators are requiring Tesla to add physical warning labels to 2.98 million Model 3 and Model Y vehicles in China explaining how to open rear doors manually during a power-loss emergency, following a growing trend of fatal crashes where occupants were trapped in burning cars with electronically controlled doors.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A 3-million-vehicle mandatory recall requiring physical dealer/service access is a material operational and cost burden for Tesla in China and signals regulators are treating electronic door handles as a systemic safety defect, not an isolated issue.
insights.locator: Tesla is facing a massive recall in China today

insights.claim: Starting next year, new Chinese rules will mandate specific handle dimensions for all newly approved vehicles, but already-sold cars like the Model 3 and Y are grandfathered in only until the end of 2028.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A firm 2028 grandfathering deadline gives a concrete regulatory timeline that could force further design or hardware changes to Tesla's China-market vehicles before then.
insights.locator: Starting next year, new rules give specific dimensions

insights.claim: In addition to physical warning labels, Tesla will push a software update to the recalled vehicles that automatically lowers all windows in the event of a collision.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A software-based mitigation (auto window-lowering) shows Tesla can partially remediate the safety issue via over-the-air update without full hardware replacement, limiting the financial severity of this specific recall.
insights.locator: Additionally, Tesla will push out a software update

insights.claim: Tesla faces a second, separate Chinese recall affecting 2.74 million cars requiring new driver-monitoring software that will use the interior camera to track driver gaze, replacing the current system which relies solely on a steering-wheel torque sensor to detect if the driver is holding the wheel.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Regulators forcing a shift from torque-sensor to camera-based gaze tracking is a meaningful safety-architecture upgrade mandate that could set a precedent other markets (including the US) may eventually follow for partially automated driving systems.
insights.locator: Tesla is also facing a second Chinese recall

insights.claim: Electrek has previously reported that Chinese Tesla owners have been able to defeat the current camera-based cabin driver-monitoring system (used with Tesla's more advanced partially automated driving feature) by mounting a doll's head in front of the camera.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A trivially defeatable driver-monitoring system undermines the safety case for Tesla's partially automated driving features in China and raises questions about whether the new gaze-tracking recall software will adequately close this loophole.
